name: Single-Cell Hall

origin.note: The irreducible unit. Nearly every Anglo-American type is an elaboration of it.

description: One heated room entered directly from outside. All domestic life - cooking, eating, sleeping, work - occurs in a single volume differentiated by furniture and habit rather than by walls.
structural_logic: A single framing bay, roughly 16-20 feet square, set by the practical span of hand-hewn joists.
expansion_logic: Grows by adding a second pen (double-pen), a lean-to at the rear (saltbox), or a second storey. Every expansion path from this cell generates a named type.
constraints: Hearth must be on an exterior wall or centred; a single-cell plan cannot carry an interior chimney without eating the room.
notes: Teaching this type first makes the rest of the catalog legible as variation rather than as a list.

name: Hall and Parlor
description: Two unequal rooms side by side: the larger hall for work and public reception, the smaller parlor for the best furniture and sleeping. The first appearance of social gradient in the Anglo house.
structural_logic: Two framing bays. Asymmetry of room size is functional, and produces the characteristic off-centre door.
expansion_logic: Adding a through-passage between the two rooms produces the center-hall plan and, with it, the entire Georgian project of symmetry.
constraints: Door placement is governed by the hall/parlor size difference, not by facade symmetry. Forcing a centred door here destroys the type.

name: Center Passage, Single Pile
description: A through-passage divides two rooms, opening front to back. The passage is a climate device as much as a circulation one: opened at both ends it draws air through the house on a summer afternoon.
structural_logic: Single room depth keeps every room cross-ventilated and daylit from two sides - the reason the type persisted in the South a century after the North had gone double-pile.
expansion_logic: Rear ell for service; or fill in behind to become double-pile at the cost of the through-draft.
constraints: Both ends of the passage must have doors or the type loses its reason for existing.

name: I-House
description: Two storeys tall, one room deep, at least two rooms wide - a tall thin slab of a house that announced a farming family's arrival at prosperity. Named for its prevalence in Indiana, Illinois, and Iowa.
structural_logic: Depth of one room means no interior bearing wall and a simple common-rafter roof; the height is pure social signalling, visible across open farmland.
expansion_logic: Almost always acquires a rear ell or kitchen wing, producing a T or L. The ell is where the house actually lived.
constraints: Reads as a facade from the road and a thin wall from the side. Any attempt to thicken it into double-pile turns it into a different type.

name: Saltbox
description: A two-storey house with a lean-to added across the rear, the roof carried down in one unbroken plane nearly to the ground on the north side. Accretion made permanent and, eventually, built that way from the start.
structural_logic: The long rear slope faces north, shedding snow and burying the coldest wall in a low, unheated service zone. Thermally intelligent before anyone used the word.
expansion_logic: This IS the expansion. Once formalized, further growth goes to an ell off the kitchen end.
constraints: The rear slope must be unbroken - dormers or a break in the plane collapse the whole figure.
Orientation matters: a saltbox with its long slope to the south is a costume, not a type.

name: Cape Cod Block
description: A low, broad, steep-roofed box hugging the ground, its massive central chimney the structural and thermal core. Sized in named increments: half, three-quarter, and full Cape, each a stage of a family's growth.
structural_logic: Low eave and steep pitch resist Atlantic wind; the central stack heats four rooms from one mass of masonry and anchors the frame.
expansion_logic: Half to three-quarter to full by adding bays to one side of the door, then dormers or an ell. The increments are the type's grammar.
constraints: Eave must sit low - within a foot or so of the second-floor sill. Raising it to gain headroom produces a different, worse house.
Central chimney is not optional; a Cape with gable-end chimneys is a different type.

name: Gambrel Block
description: A double-pitched roof buys nearly full headroom on the upper floor while keeping the eave low and the volume visually modest. The most efficient traditional answer to the problem of a second storey.
structural_logic: The break in slope allows a shorter rafter run and a usable upper floor without a full second-storey wall - a tax and material advantage as much as a spatial one.
expansion_logic: Flared eaves and a full-width shed dormer are the standard growth moves; both are period-correct if handled with restraint.
constraints: Upper slope should be roughly half the pitch of the lower; equal slopes read as a barn.
The break line should align with the upper floor level, not float arbitrarily.

name: Four-Over-Four (Georgian Double Pile)
description: Four rooms per floor around a central stair hall - the canonical Georgian box. Symmetry is not applied to this plan; it is generated by it, which is why the type survives every change of ornament.
structural_logic: Two rooms deep requires an interior bearing wall, which the stair hall supplies. Paired end chimneys serve four fireplaces per floor.
expansion_logic: Flanking dependencies connected by hyphens (the five-part scheme), or a rear service ell. Growth must respect the axis or the whole logic fails.
constraints: Facade symmetry is a hard constraint, not a preference.
Window bays must align vertically; a misaligned upper window is a structural admission that the plan is not really Georgian.

name: Five-Part Palladian
aka: main block with hyphens and dependencies
description: A dominant central block flanked by subordinate wings, joined by low connecting hyphens. Hierarchy made visible: the family in the middle, service and specialized functions stepping down and out to either side.
structural_logic: Separates the hot, smoky, and noisy from the ceremonial while keeping them connected under cover - a functional diagram before it is a compositional one.
expansion_logic: Wings may lengthen or gain a second storey, but the hierarchy of heights must be preserved. The centre must always win.
constraints: Wing ridge must sit demonstrably below the main ridge - a token difference reads as a mistake.
Hyphens must be lower and shallower than both elements they join.

name: Side-Hall Double Pile
description: Stair and passage pushed to one side, rooms lined up in an enfilade beside them. The plan that makes narrow-lot urbanism work, and the ancestor of every efficient town house since.
structural_logic: Party walls carry the load; light comes only from the two short ends, which drives room depth and the deep-parlor proportion.
expansion_logic: Vertical, not horizontal. Extra storeys, then a rear ell over the yard.
constraints: Only two elevations get windows; the plan must place service and stair where light is not needed.
Room-to-window ratio sets a maximum depth of roughly 25 feet before the middle goes dark.

name: Charleston Single House
description: One room wide and turned end-on to the street, with multi-storey piazzas running the long south or west flank behind a false street door. A climate machine disguised as a house.
structural_logic: Narrow section plus tall ceilings plus a shaded piazza produces continuous cross ventilation in a subtropical climate. Every dimension serves airflow.
expansion_logic: Lengthens to the rear; kitchen house sits detached in the yard.
constraints: Piazza must face south or west to catch the prevailing breeze and shade the long wall.
The street door opens onto the piazza, not the house - removing this move destroys the type.

name: Creole Cottage
description: A hall-less plan of four square rooms opening directly onto a full-width front gallery, with small cabinets flanking a rear loggia. No corridors: the gallery is the corridor.
structural_logic: Eliminating interior passages maximizes cross ventilation; the gallery shades the wall and keeps rain off the openings.
expansion_logic: Rear cabinet-loggia range fills in; the house grows backward, never forward past the gallery line.
constraints: Four front openings, no centred door - symmetry here is even-numbered, which reads wrong to an Anglo eye and is exactly correct.
Gallery is structural to the type, not applied.

name: Raised Cottage
description: The living floor lifted a full storey above grade on a masonry base, wrapped in deep galleries reached by a broad exterior stair. Flood response and social elevation in the same gesture.
structural_logic: Masonry base survives inundation and damp; the elevated timber floor catches breeze above the ground-level heat and insects.
expansion_logic: Gallery may wrap from front to sides; the base may be enclosed for service.
constraints: Base must read as masonry and the upper floor as lighter construction; a uniform material collapses the logic.
Stair is exterior and ceremonial.

name: Dogtrot
description: Two log pens under one roof, separated by an open central passage. The passage is the coolest place on the property in August and the reason the plan exists.
structural_logic: Log pen size is limited by log length; two pens plus a gap is cheaper and cooler than one large room. The shared roof ties them together.
expansion_logic: The breezeway is often enclosed later, converting it to a center-hall plan - the single most common type-transformation in Southern vernacular.
constraints: Passage must be open at both ends and unheated.
Pens should read as separate volumes under a shared roof.

name: Shotgun

origin.region: New Orleans, Gulf South, urban African-American communities
origin.note: West African and Haitian plan antecedents, not simply an Anglo economization.

description: One room wide and three to five rooms deep, each room opening into the next with no hallway, the gable end and its porch turned to the street. Maximum house on a minimum lot frontage.
structural_logic: Narrow lots taxed on frontage; single-pile depth keeps every room lit and ventilated from two sides with aligned doors drawing air the length of the house.
expansion_logic: Rear rooms added indefinitely; a camelback adds a second storey only at the back, preserving the street reading.
constraints: Doors must align front to back or the ventilation logic fails.
Porch is not optional - it is the house's only social space.

name: Gable Front
description: The house rotated ninety degrees so the gable faces the street, presenting a pediment-like front. Born of Greek Revival ambition and kept alive by narrow urban lots long after the temple idea faded.
structural_logic: Gable to the street fits deep narrow lots and gives a naturally pedimented facade at no extra cost.
expansion_logic: Side wing produces the gable-front-and-wing, one of the most widespread American forms.
constraints: Facade proportion should approach a pediment; too tall and narrow and it becomes a tower.

name: Gable Front and Wing

origin.region: Northeast, Midwest, and throughout rural America

description: A gable-front block with a lower side-gabled wing, the porch tucked into the inside corner. Arguably the most-built American house form of the nineteenth century and the most adaptable to any style.
structural_logic: Two simple volumes, each independently framable, joined at a right angle; the reentrant corner is a naturally sheltered entry.
expansion_logic: Wing lengthens; further ells accrete behind. The type absorbs growth gracefully, which is why it lasted a century.
constraints: Wing ridge must be lower than the main ridge.
Entry belongs in the inside corner; moving it to the gable front produces two front doors and no hierarchy.

name: Cross-Gable Block
description: Intersecting gabled volumes producing an animated roofline and a plan that can grow in three directions. The workhorse of Gothic Revival, Italianate, and Folk Victorian alike.
structural_logic: Balloon framing and machine-cut lumber made intersecting roofs cheap for the first time; the type is a direct consequence of the sawmill.
expansion_logic: Any arm may extend. Danger is unlimited growth without hierarchy.
constraints: One gable must dominate; equal arms produce an indecisive house.
Valleys are the leak points - the type demands disciplined flashing detail.

name: Massed Picturesque Block
description: A deliberately irregular agglomeration of bays, towers, porches, and projecting gables composed for the moving eye rather than the frontal view. The plan follows the picture, and occasionally the picture follows the plan.
structural_logic: Light balloon frame permits complexity that heavy timber could not afford. Complexity is the point, not a byproduct.
expansion_logic: Absorbs additions almost invisibly, which is both its great virtue and its great temptation.
constraints: Requires a dominant mass and a dominant roof or it disintegrates into noise.
Every projection must be justified by a room, not by the elevation.

name: Mansard Block
description: A full usable storey concealed within a steep-sided roof, capped by a shallow deck. Modernity in the 1860s sense: the newest fashion from Paris, and an extra floor the tax assessor once treated as attic.
structural_logic: The steep lower slope is effectively a wall carrying dormers; the flat deck above sheds to internal drains.
expansion_logic: Central or corner tower with its own mansard is the standard elaboration.
constraints: Mansard must be visually continuous around the building or it reads as a hat.
Dormer rhythm should relate to the bay rhythm below.

name: Towered Villa
description: An asymmetrical villa organized around a square tower or campanile, usually at the inner angle. The tower is a vertical accent and a stair, and it announces that this house is composed, not merely built.
structural_logic: Tower absorbs the stair and gives cross-ventilation at the top; low-pitched hips with deep bracketed eaves shade the walls.
expansion_logic: Wings extend from the tower's two faces.
constraints: Tower must rise at least a half storey above the main ridge or it is a bump.
Eave bracket rhythm should be consistent across tower and body.

name: Foursquare
description: A near-cubic two-storey box, four large rooms per floor, hipped roof with a broad central dormer, full-width front porch. The most volumetrically efficient American house ever built, and the clearest proof that massing is not style.
structural_logic: A cube has the best floor-area-to-exterior-wall ratio available to a two-storey wood frame house. Cheap to build, cheap to heat, easy to ship as a kit.
expansion_logic: Rear ell or a widened dormer. The cube itself resists distortion, which is part of its dignity.
constraints: Porch must be full width; a partial porch destroys the base of the composition.
Roof overhang must be generous - a Foursquare with clipped eaves reads as a shoebox.
notes: Routinely dressed as Craftsman, Colonial Revival, Prairie, or Mission with no change to the volume. The canonical demonstration case for separating the massing catalog from the style grammar.

name: Pyramidal Cottage
description: A single-storey square under a steep four-sided roof, four rooms around a central chimney. The economical Southern answer to a compact family house.
structural_logic: Pyramidal roof needs no ridge beam and sheds efficiently in all directions; the square plan minimizes wall length.
expansion_logic: Rear shed or ell.
constraints: Roof pitch must be steep enough to read as a pyramid rather than a hip.

name: Bungalow (Linear)

origin.note: Term via Bengali bangla by way of British India.

description: A low, ground-hugging house of one to one-and-a-half storeys, its deep porch under the main roof, its living and dining rooms flowing together around a hearth. The first mass-market American house to abandon the formal parlor.
structural_logic: Low profile, deep overhangs, and exposed structural members express the frame rather than concealing it; the whole is sized to a small urban lot.
expansion_logic: Shed dormer for upper rooms; rear ell for service. The airplane bungalow adds a single second-storey room.
constraints: Porch must be under the primary roof, not applied to it.
Eave overhang of 24-36 inches is definitional; less and it is not a bungalow.

name: Airplane Bungalow
description: A bungalow with a single small room perched centrally on the roof, windowed on all four sides - a sleeping porch or study lifted into the breeze.
structural_logic: The pop-up catches cross breezes above the roof plane; a hot-climate cooling device before mechanical air conditioning.
expansion_logic: Rarely grows; the type is complete as drawn.
constraints: Upper room must be centred and clearly subordinate.
Its roof should echo the main roof form.

name: Prairie Cruciform
description: Wings pinwheeling from a central masonry hearth, roofs low and broadly overhanging, the whole composition emphatically horizontal against a flat horizon.
structural_logic: The chimney mass is the structural and compositional anchor; cantilevered eaves shade banded windows and shed the horizontal line outward.
expansion_logic: Terraces and low walls extend the composition into the site rather than adding volume.
constraints: No vertical accent may compete with the horizontal.
Hearth must be central and expressed in mass.

name: U-Courtyard
description: Three ranges around an open court, the fourth side held by a wall or left open to a view. Rooms reached from the court rather than from interior corridors.
structural_logic: Single-pile ranges are lit and ventilated from both sides; the court moderates microclimate and provides outdoor room in hot-dry conditions.
expansion_logic: Close the fourth side to become a full courtyard; extend ranges outward.
constraints: Court must be proportioned to admit winter sun and exclude summer sun for its latitude.
Circulation through the court means the gallery must be continuous and covered.

name: Full Courtyard
description: Rooms enclose a court on all four sides, presenting a nearly blind face to the street. The house turns its back on the public world and opens entirely inward.
structural_logic: Thermal mass plus shaded court plus cross-ventilated single-pile ranges - the most durable hot-climate house diagram in existence.
expansion_logic: Second court added behind the first, service functions to the rear court.
constraints: Street elevation must be substantially closed; a courtyard house with a picture window on the street is a contradiction.
One controlled entry - the zaguan - carries the entire threshold sequence.

name: Connected Farmstead
aka: big house little house back house barn
description: House, kitchen ell, workshop, and barn joined in a continuous descending chain so that winter chores never require going outdoors. Architecture as a response to five months of snow.
structural_logic: Each link is independently framed and sized to its use; the descending ridge line sheds snow and expresses hierarchy without ornament.
expansion_logic: The type is defined by its capacity to grow - each new need becomes a new link.
constraints: Ridge heights must step down monotonically from house to barn.
Each link should be visibly a separate building, not a continuous extrusion.

name: Telescope House
description: Two to four sections of diminishing height and width strung in a line, each added as the family prospered. The house's own history is legible in its silhouette.
structural_logic: Each section is a complete small house; joining them at the gable end requires no structural negotiation.
expansion_logic: Add another, smaller section. That is the whole rule.
constraints: Each successive section must be lower AND narrower.
Sections should share a common front wall plane or a consistent setback rhythm.

name: Temple Front with Wings
description: A pedimented, colonnaded gable front flanked by lower recessed wings - the Greek temple pressed into service as a farmhouse, courthouse, and everything between.
structural_logic: Wings hold service and bedchambers so the temple block can keep its pure form; the portico shades the principal south wall.
expansion_logic: Wings lengthen or gain their own porticoes; the temple block never changes.
constraints: Portico columns must be full height of the block - a two-storey facade with one-storey columns is a different and lesser thing.
Wings must be set back from the temple front plane.

name: Octagon

origin.note: Popularized by Orson Squire Fowler's A Home for All, 1848.

description: An eight-sided house arranged around a central stair and often a central ventilating shaft, argued into existence on grounds of enclosed area per foot of wall.
structural_logic: An octagon encloses about twenty percent more area than a square of equal perimeter; the central shaft provides stack ventilation.
expansion_logic: Essentially none - the geometry is closed. A defining limitation and the reason the fashion died.
constraints: Triangular residual spaces at the corners must be programmed as closets and stairs or the plan wastes its own advantage.
notes: Included partly as a cautionary type: a massing generated by argument rather than by use, and unable to grow.

name: Row / Terrace
description: Individual houses sharing party walls in a continuous street wall. The unit is the house; the architectural subject is the block.
structural_logic: Party walls halve the exterior envelope and carry floor loads; the street wall does the urban work that no single facade can.
expansion_logic: Rear ell into the yard; vertical addition where the cornice line permits.
constraints: Cornice line, floor levels, and material must coordinate across units or the street wall fails.
Individual expression belongs at the door and window detail, not the massing.

name: Linear Ranch
description: A long, low, single-storey house stretched along the street, its garage brought into the composition and its living spaces turned to the rear yard. The first American house type designed around the automobile.
structural_logic: Single storey on a slab or crawl space, long span trusses, and a wide lot - the type is a direct expression of cheap suburban land and cheap cars.
expansion_logic: Extends at either end; rear wing to form an L.
constraints: Garage placement determines whether the street elevation is a house or a wall of doors. This is the type's central unsolved problem.
Length demands a break in plane or material every three to four bays.

name: L-Ranch
description: A ranch bent into an L, with the garage or bedroom wing turned forward to define an entry court and shelter the front door.
structural_logic: The bend creates a wind-sheltered entry and shortens the apparent street frontage of a long plan.
expansion_logic: Either leg extends; a third leg produces a U with a real forecourt.
constraints: The inside corner must hold the entry, or the L is merely a bend.

name: Split Level
description: Living, sleeping, and family zones stacked at half-storey offsets around a short central stair, usually exploiting a sloped lot.
structural_logic: Half-level offsets suit a cross-slope site and separate noisy from quiet zones without a full second storey.
expansion_logic: Poor. The section is rigid and additions rarely reconcile with the offsets.
constraints: Requires actual grade change; on a flat lot the type is arbitrary.
Roof planes at the offset are the hardest detail and the usual point of failure.

name: Double Pen
description: Two equal rooms side by side under one roof, each with its own exterior door and its own end chimney. No hierarchy, no passage - two rooms that happen to share a wall.
structural_logic: Two log or frame pens of equal size, built at once or in sequence; equality of rooms distinguishes it from hall-and-parlor.
expansion_logic: Rear shed; enclosing the two front doors into one entry converts it toward a center-hall plan.
constraints: Two front doors are definitional. One centred door makes it a different type.

name: Garrison Block
description: A two-storey box whose upper floor overhangs the lower at the front, often with turned drops at the corners - a medieval English framing habit carried across the Atlantic and long misread as a defensive feature.
structural_logic: The jetty derives from English timber framing practice, where it stiffened the frame and gained floor area; in America it survived as a decorative memory of that craft.
expansion_logic: Rear lean-to or ell.
constraints: Overhang should be modest - 10 to 18 inches. Exaggerated overhangs are a 20th-century revival exaggeration.
Overhang occurs at the front, occasionally the gable ends, never all around.

name: H-Plan Manor
description: A central hall range with projecting wings at both ends, producing an H in plan - the Tudor and Jacobean great-house diagram, descended from the medieval hall with its screens passage.
structural_logic: Single-pile ranges keep every room lit from both sides; the wings hold the two social poles, family and service, at opposite ends of the hall.
expansion_logic: Wings deepen or gain a further range; a long gallery is added at the top floor.
constraints: The hall range must remain the compositional centre.
Entry through the screens passage - offset, not centred - is the diagnostic survival of the medieval plan.

name: Gallery House
description: A compact core wrapped on one or more sides by a deep roofed gallery that carries circulation, shade, and social life. The gallery is not a porch attached to a house; the house is a core inserted into a gallery.
structural_logic: Deep shade keeps the wall out of the sun entirely; the gallery roof is often a continuation of the main roof at a broken, shallower pitch.
expansion_logic: Gallery wraps further; core deepens.
constraints: Gallery depth of 8 feet minimum - shallower and it fails as a room.
Where the gallery roof breaks pitch, the break must be consistent all around.
